claim: The neural representation of the memorandum during working memory is distributed across various cortical regions, including visual and frontal cortices.
source: When holding visual information temporarily in working memory (WM), the neural representation of the memorandum is distributed across various cortical regions, including visual and frontal cortices.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a background claim about WM representation.

claim: The role of stimulus representation in visual and frontal cortices during WM has been controversial.
source: However, the role of stimulus representation in visual and frontal cortices during WM has been controversial.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a motivation for the study.

claim: Enhanced stimulus representation in the frontal cortex tracked demands for active WM control.
source: Our results demonstrated enhanced stimulus representation in the frontal cortex that tracked demands for active WM control and enhanced stimulus representation in the visual cortex that tracked demands for precise WM maintenance.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract, supported by fMRI data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Enhanced stimulus representation in the visual cortex tracked demands for precise WM maintenance.
source: Our results demonstrated enhanced stimulus representation in the frontal cortex that tracked demands for active WM control and enhanced stimulus representation in the visual cortex that tracked demands for precise WM maintenance.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract, supported by fMRI data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Differential frontal stimulus representation traded off with the newly-generated category representation with varying control demands.
source: This differential frontal stimulus representation traded off with the newly-generated category representation with varying control demands.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract, supported by fMRI data comparing Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: Simulation using multi-module recurrent neural networks replicated human neural patterns when stimulus information was preserved for network readout.
source: Simulation using multi-module recurrent neural networks replicated human neural patterns when stimulus information was preserved for network readout.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract, supported by RNN modeling results.

claim: Flexible stimulus representation in the frontal cortex during WM serves as a potential neural coding scheme to accommodate the ever-changing environment.
source: Altogether, these findings help reconcile the long-standing debate in WM research, and provide empirical and computational evidence that flexible stimulus representation in the frontal cortex during WM serves as a potential neural coding scheme to accommodate the ever-changing environment.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the integration of fMRI and RNN findings.

claim: Real-world flexible behavior relies largely on WM, which allows the maintenance and manipulation of information in the brain in order to serve diverse behavioral goals.
source: Real-world flexible behavior relies largely on WM, which allows the maintenance and manipulation of information in the brain in order to serve diverse behavioral goals (Baddeley, 2003).
evidence: This is a background statement supported by a citation to Baddeley, 2003.

claim: Mounting evidence has demonstrated stimulus-specific representation during WM maintenance in a distributed cortical network, including sensory, parietal, and frontal cortices.
source: Over the past decade, mounting evidence has demonstrated stimulus-specific representation during WM maintenance in a distributed cortical network, including sensory, parietal, and frontal cortices (Christophel et al., 2012; Ester et al., 2015; Gosseries et al., 2018; Harrison and Tong, 2009; Riggall and Postle, 2012; Serences et al., 2009; Sprague and Serences, 2013; Yu and Shim, 2017; Yu and Shim, 2019).
evidence: This is a background statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Neurophysiological studies in non-human primates have mostly emphasized stimulus representation in the frontal cortex.
source: Specifically, while neurophysiological studies in non-human primates have mostly emphasized stimulus representation in the frontal cortex (Funahashi et al., 1989; Fuster and Alexander, 1971; Leavitt et al., 2017), neuroimaging work in humans has reported disparate findings.
evidence: This is a background statement supported by citations to primate studies.

claim: During the maintenance of simple visual features, stimulus representation is robustly encoded in the early visual cortex (EVC).
source: During the maintenance of simple visual features, stimulus representation is robustly encoded in the early visual cortex (EVC), which has been taken as the evidence in support of the sensorimotor recruitment hypothesis of WM (Harrison and Tong, 2009; Riggall and Postle, 2012; Serences et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a background statement supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: Stimulus representation in the higher-order frontoparietal cortex is typically weaker and less stable.
source: Meanwhile, stimulus representation in the higher-order frontoparietal cortex is typically weaker and less stable (Emrich et al., 2013; Gosseries et al., 2018; Riggall and Postle, 2012; Yu and Shim, 2019).
evidence: This is a background statement supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In dynamic environments such as those involving distraction, stimulus representation in EVC could be greatly interrupted or biased.
source: However, in dynamic environments such as those involving distraction, stimulus representation in EVC could be greatly interrupted or biased (Bettencourt and Xu, 2016; Hallenbeck et al., 2021; Lorenc et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a background statement supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stimulus representation in the frontal cortex could be robust under certain circumstances including attentional prioritization, categorization, and after extensive training.
source: In contrast, stimulus representation in the frontal cortex could be robust under certain circumstances including attentional prioritization (Christophel et al., 2018), categorization (Lee et al., 2013), and after extensive training (Miller et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a background statement supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Changes in stimulus representation in different cortical regions might reflect a global reconfiguration in coding strategy and resource allocation in response to varied WM functions.
source: In this study, we consider these apparent discrepancies from the perspective of cognitive flexibility (Badre et al., 2021; Fusi et al., 2016; Musslick and Cohen, 2021). We propose that changes in stimulus representation in different cortical regions might reflect a global reconfiguration in coding strategy and resource allocation in response to varied WM functions (Henderson et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study, supported by citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: Stimulus representation in frontal cortex should be enhanced for active-control-related functions in WM.
source: First, in accordance with the findings of elevated neural activity in the frontal cortex with increasing demand for memory manipulation (D'Esposito et al., 1999, D'Esposito et al., 2000) and cognitive control (Badre, 2008; Badre et al., 2010; Miller and Cohen, 2001), stimulus representation in frontal cortex should be enhanced for active-control-related functions in WM.
evidence: This is a prediction of the study, supported by citations to previous findings.

claim: Stimulus representation in visual cortex should be enhanced for precise-maintenance-related functions in WM.
source: By contrast, due to the precise nature of stimulus representation in visual cortex, stimulus representation in this region should be enhanced for precise-maintenance-related functions in WM (Henderson et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a prediction of the study, supported by citations to previous findings.

claim: A dynamic tradeoff between representations of original and new information should be observed within the brain regions that encode the newly generated information.
source: Second, within the brain regions that encode the newly generated information, a dynamic tradeoff between representations of original and new information should be observed to achieve a flexible allocation of limited cognitive resources (Badre et al., 2021; Flesch et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a prediction of the study, supported by citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: Participants acquired the two categorization rules with equal familiarity.
source: Participants acquired the two rules with equal familiarity (t(23) = 0.24, p=0.813; for Rule A, M=0.85, SD = 0.050; for Rule B, M=0.85, SD = 0.05; Figure 1C)
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the learning session, supported by statistical test and Figure 1C.

claim: Participants acquired the two categorization rules with comparable precision.
source: and comparable precision (averaged error in reported boundaries for Rule A were 8.80°±6.29° and that for Rule B was 9.02°±5.69°; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the learning session, supported by data and Figure 1D.

claim: Accuracy for the maintenance task and that for the categorization task did not significantly differ.
source: Accuracy for the maintenance task (M ± SD: 0.81±0.07) and that for the categorization task (0.82±0.05) did not significantly differ (t(23) = 1.51, p=0.144; Figure 1E)
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the fMRI session, supported by statistical test and Figure 1E.

claim: The two tasks were matched in terms of task difficulty.
source: Accuracy for the maintenance task (M ± SD: 0.81±0.07) and that for the categorization task (0.82±0.05) did not significantly differ (t(23) = 1.51, p=0.144; Figure 1E), suggesting that the two tasks were matched in terms of task difficulty.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral results, based on the lack of accuracy difference.

claim: Only in the categorization task but not in the maintenance task did participants perform better for trials distant from category boundaries in terms of both accuracy and reaction time.
source: In line with previous categorization studies demonstrating a boundary effect (Ester et al., 2020; Freedman and Assad, 2006), only in the categorization task but not in the maintenance task did participants perform better for trials distant from category boundaries in terms of both accuracy and reaction time (see Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a behavioral result demonstrating the boundary effect, supported by Figure 1G and citations to previous studies.

claim: The boundary effect results demonstrated the effect of categorization and confirmed that participants faithfully followed task instructions.
source: These results demonstrated the effect of categorization and confirmed that participants faithfully followed task instructions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the boundary effect results.

claim: Significant orientation representation was observed in EVC in both maintenance and categorization tasks starting from the sample period.
source: In EVC, we found significant orientation representation in both maintenance and categorization tasks starting from the sample period (Figure 2C left panel; see Figure 2—source data 1 for full statistics)
evidence: This is a primary fMRI finding, supported by Figure 2C and statistical data.

claim: The strength of orientation representation in the maintenance task became significantly higher than that in the categorization task after the task cue during the delay in EVC.
source: Additionally, the strength of orientation representation in the maintenance task became significantly higher than that in the categorization task after the task cue during the delay, suggesting the strength of orientation representations in EVC reflected the degrees of task demands for maintaining visual details.
evidence: This is a primary fMRI finding from EVC, supported by Figure 2C.

claim: The strength of orientation representations in EVC reflected the degrees of task demands for maintaining visual details.
source: Additionally, the strength of orientation representation in the maintenance task became significantly higher than that in the categorization task after the task cue during the delay, suggesting the strength of orientation representations in EVC reflected the degrees of task demands for maintaining visual details.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EVC results.

claim: In IPS, orientation representation was significant in both tasks, but did not differ from each other at most time points.
source: In IPS, orientation representation was significant in both tasks, but did not differ from each other at most time points (Figure 2C middle panel).
evidence: This is a primary fMRI finding from IPS, supported by Figure 2C.

claim: In sPCS, in the maintenance task, orientation information was maintained during early delay period and then dropped to baseline level during late delay period.
source: In sPCS, a reversed pattern was observed. In the maintenance task, orientation information was maintained during early delay period and then dropped to baseline level during late delay period.
evidence: This is a primary fMRI finding from sPCS, supported by Figure 2C.

claim: In sPCS, in the categorization task, orientation representation was persistent throughout the delay and response periods.
source: By contrast, in the categorization task, orientation representation was persistent throughout the delay and response periods.
evidence: This is a primary fMRI finding from sPCS, supported by Figure 2C.

claim: The strength of orientation representation in the categorization task became statistically higher than that in the maintenance task in late delay period in sPCS.
source: The strength of orientation representation in the categorization task became statistically higher than that in the maintenance task in late delay period (Figure 2C right panel), suggesting that this differential representations of visual stimulus in the frontal cortex reflected the demand for active control of memory contents.
evidence: This is a primary fMRI finding from sPCS, supported by Figure 2C.

claim: The differential representations of visual stimulus in the frontal cortex reflected the demand for active control of memory contents.
source: The strength of orientation representation in the categorization task became statistically higher than that in the maintenance task in late delay period (Figure 2C right panel), suggesting that this differential representations of visual stimulus in the frontal cortex reflected the demand for active control of memory contents.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the sPCS results.

claim: The strength of stimulus representation in EVC during the early delay period predicted behavioral accuracies in both maintenance and categorization tasks.
source: Consistent with previous findings, we found the strength of stimulus representation in EVC during the early delay period predicted behavioral accuracies in both maintenance and categorization tasks (see Figure 3—source data 1 for full statistics).
evidence: This is a brain-behavior correlation result, supported by Figure 3 and statistical data.

claim: Stimulus representation in IPS predicted behavior in the maintenance task during early delay and in the categorization task throughout the entire memory delay.
source: Similar predictability was found in IPS, with stimulus representation predicted behavior in the maintenance task during early delay and in the categorization task throughout the entire memory delay.
evidence: This is a brain-behavior correlation result, supported by Figure 3.

claim: Throughout the entire memory delay, the strength of stimulus representation in sPCS predicted behavioral accuracies only in the categorization task but not in the maintenance task.
source: Interestingly, we found that, throughout the entire memory delay, the strength of stimulus representation in sPCS predicted behavioral accuracies only in the categorization task but not in the maintenance task.
evidence: This is a brain-behavior correlation result, supported by Figure 3.

claim: The behavioral predictability results highlighted the functional significance of stimulus representation in sPCS exclusively for the categorization task.
source: These results highlighted the functional significance of stimulus representation in sPCS exclusively for the categorization task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the brain-behavior correlation results.

claim: EVC and IPS both showed patterns similar to those in Experiment 1 in Experiment 2.
source: When using IEMs to reconstruct stimulus representation, we found EVC and IPS both showed patterns similar to those in Experiment 1 (Figure 4A left and middle panels), with stimulus representation decreased in EVC in the categorization task and remained at the same level in IPS between the two tasks (see Figure 4—source data 1 for full statistics).
evidence: This is a comparison of fMRI results between Experiments 1 and 2, supported by Figure 4A.

claim: The frontal region, sPCS, showed a differential enhancement of stimulus representation in the categorization task as in Experiment 1, but in an earlier period in Experiment 2.
source: The frontal region, sPCS, also showed a differential enhancement of stimulus representation in the categorization task as in Experiment 1, but in an earlier period (Figure 4A right panel).
evidence: This is a comparison of fMRI results between Experiments 1 and 2, supported by Figure 4A.

claim: There was a significant difference in stimulus representation in sPCS during the early epoch but not during the late epoch in Experiment 2.
source: To validate such a temporal difference, we defined an additional early task epoch (5–10 s), and confirmed a significant difference in stimulus representation in sPCS during the early (p=0.015; Figure 4B) but not during the late epoch (p=0.372; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2, supported by Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: A mixed ANOVA on experiments (Experiment 1 vs 2) and epochs (early vs. late epoch) observed a significant interaction effect between the two.
source: In addition, we performed a mixed ANOVA on experiments (Experiment 1 vs 2) and epochs (early vs. late epoch) and observed a significant interaction effect between the two, F(1, 46)=7.43, p=0.009, suggesting that the two experiments differed in terms of the temporal emergence of the differential stimulus representation in the frontal cortex.
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: The two experiments differed in terms of the temporal emergence of the differential stimulus representation in the frontal cortex.
source: In addition, we performed a mixed ANOVA on experiments (Experiment 1 vs 2) and epochs (early vs. late epoch) and observed a significant interaction effect between the two, F(1, 46)=7.43, p=0.009, suggesting that the two experiments differed in terms of the temporal emergence of the differential stimulus representation in the frontal cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ANOVA result.

claim: With reduced control demand, the differential enhancement of stimulus representation in frontal cortex was still present but decreased during late memory delay.
source: Taken together, these results are consistent with our expectation that, with reduced control demand, the differential enhancement of stimulus representation in frontal cortex was still present but decreased during late memory delay.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Experiment 2 results.

claim: During the late epoch, category information could be well decoded across ROIs in both experiments.
source: In both experiments, we found that during the late epoch, category information could be well decoded across ROIs (ps <0.044, Figure 5A; also see Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for full decoding time course)
evidence: This is a category decoding result, supported by Figure 5A.

claim: There was a marginal difference in category decoding between experiments in sPCS.
source: In both experiments, we found that during the late epoch, category information could be well decoded across ROIs (ps <0.044, Figure 5A; also see Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for full decoding time course), with a marginal difference between experiments in sPCS (p=0.055).
evidence: This is a category decoding result, supported by Figure 5A.

claim: After removing stimulus-related signals, average decoding performance of abstract category was only evident in Experiment 2 but not in Experiment 1 for all ROIs.
source: After removing stimulus-related signals, average decoding performance of abstract category was only evident in Experiment 2 (ps <0.017) but not in Experiment 1 (ps >0.14) for all ROIs.
evidence: This is an abstract category decoding result, supported by Figure 5D.

claim: Decoding performance of abstract category was significantly higher in Experiment 2 than Experiment 1 in sPCS.
source: Moreover, decoding performance of abstract category was significantly higher in Experiment 2 than Experiment 1 in sPCS (P=0.034; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an abstract category decoding result, supported by Figure 5D.

claim: The abstract category results suggest a potential tradeoff between stimulus difference and category representation in the frontal cortex.
source: These results together suggest a potential tradeoff between stimulus difference and category representation in the frontal cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the abstract category decoding results.

claim: The LMEM results replicated the above findings, with significant stimulus but not category representation in sPCS in Experiment 1, and a decreased contribution of stimulus but emerging category representation in the same brain region in Experiment 2.
source: Overall, the LMEM results (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–D) replicated the above findings, with significant stimulus but not category representation in sPCS in Experiment 1, and a decreased contribution of stimulus but emerging category representation in the same brain region in Experiment 2.
evidence: This is a result from the LMEM analysis, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: In RNN1, both the middle and anterior modules showed stronger stimulus representation in the maintenance task than the categorization task during the delay period.
source: We found that in RNN1, both the middle and anterior modules showed stronger stimulus representation in the maintenance task than the categorization task during the delay period (pposterior = 0.09,pmiddle = 0.011, panterior = 0.007; Figure 6B upper panel), opposite to our fMRI observation in IPS and sPCS (Figure 6B inset).
evidence: This is a result from the RNN1 modeling, supported by Figure 6B.

claim: Decoding performance in RNN2 yielded results consistent with human findings, with increased stimulus decoding performance during categorization only in the anterior module.
source: In comparison, decoding performance in RNN2, which was explicitly required to maintain stimulus information for the output, yielded results consistent with our human findings, with increased stimulus decoding performance during categorization only in the anterior module (pposterior = 0.436, pmiddle = 0.212, panterior = 0.026; Figure 6B lower panel).
evidence: This is a result from the RNN2 modeling, supported by Figure 6B.

claim: Consistent with human findings, increased abstract category decoding performance was observed in the fixed-rule models compared to the flexible-rule RNNs, throughout the modules.
source: Consistent with our human findings, we observed increased abstract category decoding performance in the fixed-rule models compared to the flexible-rule RNNs, throughout the modules (pposterior = 0.045, pmiddle = 0.003, panterior <0.001; Figure 6C lower panel).
evidence: This is a result from the RNN modeling comparing flexible and fixed rules, supported by Figure 6C.

claim: RNN2 consistently demonstrated higher similarity to human data than RNN1, particularly in Module 3 that corresponds to the frontal cortex.
source: Overall, across experiments, RNN2 consistently demonstrated higher similarity to human data than RNN1, particularly in Module 3 that corresponds to the frontal cortex (Figure 7B and D).
evidence: This is a result from the RSA between RNN and human data, supported by Figures 7B and 7D.

claim: RNN2 exhibited stronger stimulus representation than RNN1.
source: In terms of the RDM patterns, consistent with previous results, RNN2 exhibited stronger stimulus representation than RNN1.
evidence: This is a result from the RDM analysis of RNN models.

claim: Fixed-rule RNNs were found to be more categorical than flexible-rule RNNs regardless of the output structure.
source: Moreover, fixed-rule RNNs were found to be more categorical than flexible-rule RNNs regardless of the output structure.
evidence: This is a result from the RDM analysis of RNN models.

claim: The fMRI results could be simulated by RNN models when stimulus information for readout was preserved.
source: Altogether, these findings demonstrated that our fMRI results could be simulated by RNN models when stimulus information for readout was preserved, suggesting that the requirement for flexible control of WM content could demand high-fidelity stimulus representation at the output stage of the model.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the RNN modeling results.

claim: The requirement for flexible control of WM content could demand high-fidelity stimulus representation at the output stage of the model.
source: Altogether, these findings demonstrated that our fMRI results could be simulated by RNN models when stimulus information for readout was preserved, suggesting that the requirement for flexible control of WM content could demand high-fidelity stimulus representation at the output stage of the model.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the RNN modeling results.

claim: RNN2 generally took fewer iterations for training and had fewer failures in learning the task.
source: Notably, we found that RNN2 generally took fewer iterations for training and had fewer failures in learning the task (with a defined maximal number of iterations).
evidence: This is an observation from the RNN training process.

claim: The visual cortex has been considered a critical site for maintaining visual WM in the context of sensorimotor recruitment hypothesis.
source: The visual cortex has been considered a critical site for maintaining visual WM in the context of sensorimotor recruitment hypothesis (D'Esposito and Postle, 2015; Harrison and Tong, 2009).
evidence: This is a background statement supported by citations.

claim: Compared to the frontoparietal cortex, mnemonic representations in EVC were found to be more vulnerable to distractors.
source: For example, compared to the frontoparietal cortex, mnemonic representations in EVC were found to be more vulnerable to distractors (Bettencourt and Xu, 2016; Hallenbeck et al., 2021; Lorenc et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a background statement supported by citations.

claim: In nonvisual tasks that required judgments on object category instead of visual details, memory contents were no longer decodable in the visual cortex.
source: A previous study showed that in nonvisual tasks that required judgments on object category instead of visual details, memory contents were no longer decodable in the visual cortex (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a background statement supported by a citation.

claim: Although the strength of stimulus representation in EVC differed between WM maintenance and categorization tasks, a copy of stimulus representation remained in EVC during the categorization task.
source: In this study, we found that, although the strength of stimulus representation in EVC differed between WM maintenance and categorization tasks, a copy of stimulus representation remained in EVC during the categorization task.
evidence: This is a summary of the EVC findings from the current study.

claim: Stimulus representations in both tasks were equally predictive of subsequent memory performance in EVC.
source: Moreover, stimulus representations in both tasks were equally predictive of subsequent memory performance, suggesting the functional significance of EVC representations in WM.
evidence: This is a summary of the brain-behavior correlation findings in EVC.

claim: The finding is consistent with the prediction of sensorimotor recruitment hypothesis that representation of memory contents in the visual cortex is necessary for the precise maintenance of visual information.
source: Our finding is consistent with the prediction of sensorimotor recruitment hypothesis that representation of memory contents in the visual cortex is necessary for the precise maintenance of visual information.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EVC findings in relation to existing theory.

claim: The observation of robust category representation in EVC during the response period further indicated the recruitment of EVC in categorization, possibly for boundary comparison and rule implementation.
source: The observation of robust category representation in EVC during the response period further indicated the recruitment of EVC in categorization, possibly for boundary comparison and rule implementation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the category representation findings in EVC.

claim: The results are consistent with a recent study demonstrating significant stimulus representation in EVC even when memoranda had been transformed into a motor format.
source: In fact, our results are consistent with a recent study demonstrating significant stimulus representation in EVC even when memoranda had been transformed into a motor format (Henderson et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with a previous study, supported by a citation.

claim: Electrophysiological research in non-human primates has shown robust feature selectivity in the visual cortex during a categorization task.
source: In addition, electrophysiological research in non-human primates has also shown robust feature selectivity in the visual cortex during a categorization task (Brincat et al., 2018)
evidence: This is a background statement supported by a citation.

claim: Recent computational modeling work has suggested intact maintenance of sensory information during categorical judgments.
source: and recent computational modeling work has suggested intact maintenance of sensory information during categorical judgments (Luu and Stocker, 2021).
evidence: This is a background statement supported by a citation.

claim: sPCS in the frontal cortex played a dominant role in WM tasks that require active control of memory contents such as categorization.
source: Compared to the prominent role of EVC in memory maintenance, sPCS in the frontal cortex played a dominant role in WM tasks that require active control of memory contents such as categorization.
evidence: This is a summary of the sPCS findings from the current study.

claim: In WM tasks that required mere maintenance of memoranda, stimulus was not always decodable in the frontal cortex.
source: In WM tasks that required mere maintenance of memoranda, stimulus was not always decodable in the frontal cortex (Emrich et al., 2013; Gosseries et al., 2018; Riggall and Postle, 2012)
evidence: This is a background statement supported by citations.

claim: Stimulus representation in the frontal cortex could become robust in the face of tasks that require attentional prioritization and extensive training.
source: On the other hand, stimulus representation in the frontal cortex could become robust in the face of tasks that require attentional prioritization and extensive training (Bettencourt and Xu, 2016; Christophel et al., 2018; Hallenbeck et al., 2021; Lorenc et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a background statement supported by citations.

claim: The current study contributes to the resolution of the issue of functional significance of stimulus representation in the frontal cortex by demonstrating that stimulus representation in sPCS increased with increasing demands for WM control.
source: Our current study contributes to the resolution of this issue by demonstrating that stimulus representation in sPCS increased with increasing demands for WM control.
evidence: This is a summary of the contribution of the current study.

claim: This finding is in line with recent computational studies proposing that active WM functions may involve neuronal mechanisms different from that for passive maintenance.
source: This finding is in line with recent computational studies proposing that active WM functions may involve neuronal mechanisms different from that for passive maintenance.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with computational theories.

claim: Passive maintenance could rely mainly on synaptic plasticity mechanisms, whereas active control functions such as distractor resistance and information manipulation involve more neuronal spiking activity.
source: For example, passive maintenance could rely mainly on synaptic plasticity mechanisms, whereas active control functions such as distractor resistance and information manipulation involve more neuronal spiking activity (Masse et al., 2019; Wang, 2021).
evidence: This is a background statement about computational theories, supported by citations.

claim: The study provided the first empirical evidence that the frontal cortex exhibits enhanced stimulus representation in categorization task requiring active WM control and this representation is predictive of WM performance.
source: In this study, we provided the first empirical evidence that the frontal cortex exhibits enhanced stimulus representation in categorization task requiring active WM control and this representation is predictive of WM performance.
evidence: This is a summary of the main contribution of the study.

claim: Stimulus representation of WM maintenance failed to predict WM performance at high control demand in the frontal cortex.
source: In contrast, stimulus representation of WM maintenance failed to predict WM performance at high control demand.
evidence: This is a summary of the brain-behavior correlation findings in sPCS.

claim: Results in iPCS, IFS, and MFG were overall weaker, with the MFG demonstrating the most comparable, albeit much weaker, results to sPCS.
source: Moreover, by examining additional ROIs in the frontal cortex (i.e. iPCS, IFS, and MFG), we found that results in these brain regions were overall weaker, with the MFG demonstrating the most comparable, albeit much weaker, results to sPCS.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings in additional frontal ROIs.

claim: The specific involvement of sPCS in the experiment could be due to the type of stimulus (i.e. orientation) used.
source: The specific involvement of sPCS in our experiment could be due to the type of stimulus (i.e. orientation) we used, as previous work has highlighted a prominent role of sPCS in encoding stimulus-specific information in spatial (Hallenbeck et al., 2021; Sprague and Serences, 2013) and orientation WM (Ester et al., 2015; Yu and Shim, 2017; Yu and Shim, 2019), but to a lesser extent in other WM tasks such as color (Yu and Shim, 2017; Yu and Shim, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation about the specificity of sPCS involvement, supported by citations.

claim: The results in the frontal cortex are in line with recent theoretical proposals in the field of cognitive flexibility.
source: Our results in the frontal cortex are also in line with recent theoretical proposals in the field of cognitive flexibility.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with theoretical frameworks.

claim: Two mechanisms have been proposed for flexible behavior: low-dimensional abstraction of stimulus representation for generalization and efficient learning, and high-dimensional stimulus representation for separability and flexible readout.
source: To behave flexibly in complex environments with limited cognitive resources, two mechanisms have been proposed: low-dimensional abstraction of stimulus representation for generalization and efficient learning, and high-dimensional stimulus representation for separability and flexible readout (Badre et al., 2021; Flesch et al., 2022; Fusi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a background statement about theoretical frameworks, supported by citations.

claim: High-dimensional stimulus representation during WM might emerge in the frontal cortex in response to complex control demands such as rule-based categorization.
source: Within this framework, high-dimensional stimulus representation during WM might emerge in the frontal cortex in response to complex control demands such as rule-based categorization.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings within a theoretical framework.

claim: The results of the two fMRI experiments jointly demonstrate a dynamic tradeoff between high-dimensional stimulus and low-dimensional category representations depending on the control demand.
source: The results of the two fMRI experiments in the current study jointly demonstrate a dynamic tradeoff between high-dimensional stimulus and low-dimensional category representations depending on the control demand.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from both experiments.

claim: When control demand was reduced with a single categorization rule in Experiment 2 compared to Experiment 1, the differential stimulus representation in the frontal cortex was also reduced during the late delay period, accompanied by an increase in category decoding performance especially in the frontal cortex.
source: Specifically, when control demand was reduced with a single categorization rule in Experiment 2 compared to Experiment 1, the differential stimulus representation in the frontal cortex was also reduced during the late delay period, accompanied by an increase in category decoding performance especially in the frontal cortex.
evidence: This is a summary of the comparison between Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: This result is consistent with neurophysiological findings in non-human primates showing robust category selectivity in frontoparietal cortex during the delay period of categorization tasks when the animal was trained on the categorization task only.
source: This result is consistent with neurophysiological findings in non-human primates: while robust category selectivity was observed in frontoparietal cortex during the delay period of categorization tasks when the animal was trained on the categorization task only (Brincat et al., 2018; Freedman and Assad, 2006; Freedman et al., 2001; McKee et al., 2014)
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with primate studies, supported by citations.

claim: Category selectivity in the parietal cortex was significantly reduced when the animal had been exposed to a maintenance task prior to categorization training.
source: category selectivity in the parietal cortex was significantly reduced when the animal had been exposed to a maintenance task prior to categorization training (Latimer and Freedman, 2023).
evidence: This is a background statement supported by a citation.

claim: The RNN simulation confirmed that the dynamic reconfiguration in information coding at the network level can be well explained by a change in the coding strategy for the network readout.
